lignes.texte: Washington just lost the biggest gamble in financial history.
For over a decade, policymakers have run America on ultra cheap,
short term debt betting that near zero interest rates would last forever.
That bet just lost.
For the first time ever, America’s annual interest crossed $1.25 trillion,
officially eclipsing the national defense budget. Taxpayer money was sucked into past
borrowing before a penny can be spent repairing roads, upgrading schools or building hospitals.
It’s not a future crisis. It’s already here… and DC isn’t picking up the tab.
You are.
Across the 2025 budget year, Washington burned through $970 billion in interest
alone. Not a single dollar went to improving the country. Instead,
it was covering loans taken out years ago.
That works out to $2,800 taken away from every single American.
You didn’t vote for these charges. You didn’t agree to them. But your employer
withheld them from your paycheck before you even saw a dime. Today,
nearly a fifth of everything the government collects is immediately
handed over to bondholders, foreign nations and Wall Street hedge funds.
A dollar spent on defense helps fund a warship. A dollar funneled
into Medicaid helps provide a hospital visit. A dollar spent on interest buys
absolutely nothing. Americans are paying the price for years of reckless spending.
The country is in a financial doom loop.
The U.S. is officially borrowing new money just to pay off the interest on its old money. In 2022,
the interest on the debt was $476 billion. In just 3 years, it has more than doubled.
But this economic disaster didn’t happen by accident.
It was engineered.
Every time the Treasury borrows, a clock starts ticking.
They can lock in a 30-year bond, just like a fixed rate mortgage. Or they can
take a risk on short paper, loans that are due in a few months or years. For years,
the Treasury rolled debt over at shockingly low rates, treating it like free cash.
It seemed like a good idea at the time. By picking the low rate option, they saved billion.
But now, that ticking clock just ran out.
And the Treasury is forced to renegotiate those trillions of dollars at today’s crippling rates.
2022 was a brutal year for borrowers but it was unprecedented for the government.
The interest rates they used to rely on skyrocketed and lenders demanded their
money right away. The government only survived by doubling down.
The country's debt burden was already heavy.
The debt repricing only made it worse.
Normally this kind of crisis happens during a war or a devastating recession. But the economy at the
time was strong and unemployment low. But the government was still spending beyond its means.
It all reached a breaking point in July 2026. The government faced the
fourth worst spending month in American history,
spending $432 billion more than it raised. Debt is being piled on top of debt.
Now it’s catching up on them.
It’s easy to blame public spending for all of this. But freezing government
programs wouldn’t actually help. The interest is the problem.
Interest spending was 8.7% of total tax receipts in 2021. By the end of 2025,
it had nearly doubled to 18.5%. That’s the highest it’s been since the early 90s. But back then,
the debt burden was low, even though interest rates were high. Today, it’s the opposite.
Rates are low, but the monumental debt burden makes things more expensive.
Right now, interest eats up 3.3% of the country's GDP. According to the
current trajectory, it will be at 4.6% by 2036.
It’s even worse than it seems.
A large part of federal revenue is the payroll tax, devoted to Social Security. After removing
that, interest effectively swallows a quarter of the remaining revenue. It’s like a household
bringing in $60,000 in a year. Before any money is spent on groceries, there’s a $12,000 bill for
credit card interest. No one would consider that to be a financially stable household.
About a third of what the Treasury owes to the public is due by the
end of 2027. That comes to roughly $9.7 trillion that has to be paid back this
year. And the Treasury desperately has to find a buyer for all of it.
Washington doesn’t have the luxury of picking and choosing when to refinance. It’s dictated
by the timeline, no matter how bad interest rates are. As a result, the average rate the
government pays continues to increase, despite what the Fed does. Each time they sell off bonds,
they’re getting higher and higher rates. That money has to come from somewhere.
Each year around $112 billion is spent by the federal government. Interest payments outpace
that by roughly 9 to 1. School districts are feeling the effects before Washington
does. Public lands and national parks are being outpaced by an even greater margin.
America’s infrastructure is being swallowed by a financial black hole.
It’s voracious.
None of this gets called a cut. Programs are just dropped and nobody has to give an explanation.
But the government's own books aren't the only ones feeling the squeeze. Treasury yields set the
floor for nearly every loan in the U.S. Mortgages, car loans, and credit card debts all sit on it.
In August 2026, the 30 year treasury yield hit 5.31%. At the same time, the government was
selling 30-year bonds with a yield of 5.21%, the steepest yield at any auction since 2001.
That shows up in mortgage and loan payments for ordinary Americans.
Just a quarter point on a $350,000 loan is about $55 a month. That's $660 a year,
and it sounds survivable until you realize it came from borrowing decisions over
a decade ago. When Washington borrows more, so does the rest of the country.
The government uses your money to pay interest and raises the cost of your own debt in the process.
For 80 years, this was never an issue.
All over the world, there was a demand for dollars, and the safest place to
park cash was a U.S. Treasury bond. Central banks would buy U.S. Treasury bonds in the
trillions without ever worrying about the price. Even now, Tokyo's government holds
about $1.1 trillion of these bonds, making them a load-bearing part of your tax bill.
But that global loyalty is cracking.
The auctions happen every week. Only a few banks are required to
make a bid. Every other potential buyer in the world has to decide if the yield
is worth the risk. And lately those global buyers are saying “no thanks.”
When a bond sale doesn't go well, traders call it a "tail." It’s a polite way of saying it’s
a disaster. It means buyers didn’t turn up, so the government had to sweeten the
deal by offering higher interest rates just to get the money. And it’s the taxpayers who
have to pay off those sweetened, high interest rates for the next 30 years.
In August 2026, the Treasury tried to sell off $16 billion of 20-year bonds.
To say demand was low is being kind. The preferred buyers were turning their backs
on the bonds. So it was left to the banks of last resort, the dealers required to bid,
snapping up 12.5% of the sale, well above the normal amounts.
The free market was running away.
And alarm bells were ringing in Washington.
On August 19th, the Treasury Department announced that it would at least double
the size of its buyback operations, increasing them from $2 billion to
$4 billion. The next day, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent appeared on
television and said that his department would make a market for its own debt.
The government department tasked with auctioning off bonds admitted no one wanted to buy the
bonds. So, they’re using their own cash to buy their own debt… just to prop up the market.
They changed this rule pretty quickly, just days after long yields reached a 19-year high.
Sellers were panicking, already waiting to unload American debt. Investors tried
to dump $95 billion of long bonds onto a government program with a limit of $8
billion. The government bought what it could, but had to reject the rest. That leaves a lot
of people trying to get rid of the bonds they don’t want. And that the taxpayers are servicing.
The same thing happened with the shorter end of the bond. Investors offered $50
billion of 10-20 year bonds for operations with a limit of $6 billion. Once again,
the limit was the only thing that stopped more bonds being unloaded.
The Treasury can’t print money out of thin air to buy back the long term bonds. To get the cash,
they have to sell the short term loans over the space of a few months. Sound familiar?
It’s the same situation that started this crisis in the first place. Washington is
pouring gasoline on the fire, just because the payments look smaller at this time.
Of course, a $4 billion buy back is nothing compared to the $31.4 trillion of marketable
debt. It’s barely a tenth of a percent of what is outstanding. Anyone claiming
that the bond market broke in August 2026 is trying to sell you something.
What is important is that the government tried it at all. These emergency debt buy
backs started in 2024 as a behind the scenes technical tool. But they were run multiple
times throughout 2025. By the end of the year, the operation had more than doubled in size.
You don’t take that kind of risk unless the market is actively rejecting you.
The privilege of being the world’s reserve currency hasn’t been taken away from America.
It’s just that the world is charging the U.S. more to keep it that way.
This is where the most obvious answer comes in,
and it is the answer that every comment section arrives at.
So why doesn’t the Fed just cut rates?
First, the Federal Reserve is operating with handcuffs on. They have kept rates
at 3.5 to 3.75% for 5 consecutive meetings. During the last meeting,
3 of their own members voted to increase rates. Inflation was still 3.5% in June 2026,
which was well above the Federal Reserve's safe target of 2%..
Even if the Fed caved and slashed rates, the relief would be less than people think.
It wouldn’t save the nation.
Lowering the Fed's daily interest rate doesn’t affect the contracts or bonds that
have already been sold. It doesn’t shrink the $32 trillion in bonds that the public already holds.
If the Fed cuts because the economy is stalling, your paycheck shrinks along
with the government’s tax revenue. While the dollar cost of debt service may decrease,
the share of interest cost to the government actually worsens.
But what if the Fed cuts rates purely to bail out the Treasury?
Lenders all over the world will notice immediately. They’ll realize that the
government is willing to sacrifice the dollar just to keep its head above water. To protect
themselves, lenders would demand even higher rates before buying any more American bonds.
Long term rates will keep rising, and refinancing the country’s debt will be even harder.
It’s a scenario known as fiscal dominance. It’s when a government's runaway budget comes
before everything else, including the ability to keep prices stable.
It’s happened in the United States before.
During and after the Second World War, the Federal Reserve lowered interest
rates to help the Treasury. Bonds didn't default, but their value was completely
wiped out because of inflation. Anyone who bought a war bond got their money,
but those dollars covered a small fraction of what the bond was worth.
The government is faced with two options. The first is accept the higher rates and
watch the budget get cannibalized. Or let the currency lose value and use
the hyper inflated, cheaper dollars to settle the debt.
The first option eats into public services.
The second option eats into your personal savings.
None of this means America is about to default on its debt. And that’s important.
The United States borrows in a currency it creates out of thin air. It will make every
single payment, on time and in full. And it will continue to do so for a long time.
And that’s why the risk is so dangerous.
A country that is always able to print more money will never experience a dramatic, Hollywood style
economic collapse. Interest will keep growing, and the room for everything else will keep shrinking.
The money in your account will buy less every year.
And it’s already happening.
Your grocery bill increases by a few percent. Your rent or your mortgage
payment increases. Your boss gives you a smaller raise… or none at all. It’s small,
incremental changes. But over the course of a decade, the impact hits home. Losing
3% of your value each year means that every $10,000 saved is only worth around $7,400.
Your statement will still show it is worth $10,000.
But your spending power is weaker.
By 2036, the Congressional Budget Office, or CBO,
expects interest to reach almost $2.1 trillion. Measured against revenue,
that's over a quarter of everything the government brings in. By the 2050s, under current policies,
interest payments will consume 37% of all the money the government takes in. Over the
next decade, America will pay $16.2 trillion in interest. That's close to double what the country
spent on interest across the previous two decades combined, even after adjusting for inflation.
The problem is spiraling out of control.
And no one can stop it.
All those forecasts rely on the belief that interest rates will stay low. Even just a small
1% increase in the average interest rate would instantly add hundreds of billions of dollars
in extra costs each year. That’s the equivalent of funding an entire second U.S. military budget,
covering it with taxes… and getting no protection or benefit in return.
It now costs around $117,000 per person in the U.S. to pay off
the national debt. That means the average household owes $297,000.
That's what an extended period of cheap money has bought us.
A bill landing on the doorstep of every single American.
Washington took advantage of historically low interest rates to borrow massive amounts of
money. It opted to pay the short-term notes because the principal and interest payments
seemed small. The government has locked in a long-term liability, committing to refinance it on
a secondary market that resets every day and charges whatever the market determines.
Interest is now the third largest thing the federal government does with money, ahead of every
other agency and every program. Interest payments are made before any other payments are made,
and the amount that is withheld from your pay regardless if the economy is strong or weak.
Washington gambled with America's money… and lost.
And now the debt is being called in.
The U.S. debt is out of control and it’s threatening the livelihood of
